claims.text: Multistage thermo-mechanical processing can generate a stepwise sequence of disparate coherent nano-precipitates in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The proposed intervention applies to refractory high-entropy alloys having a dual-phase structure.
The resulting precipitates are coherent and have disparate nanoscale structures.
Coherent nano-precipitates strengthen the alloy through precipitation hardening.
The intervention produces progressive multistage strain hardening.
The intervention can produce ultrahigh yield strength at both ambient and elevated temperatures.
The intervention can retain tensile ductility at both ambient and elevated temperatures.
The predicted strength and ductility combination extends to 800 °C.
The precipitate strategy improves mechanical performance relative to traditional single-principal-element metallurgical design approaches.
Traditional single-principal-element approaches have difficulty achieving alloys that are simultaneously very strong, ductile, and stable at high temperature.
The intervention maintains thermal stability during high-temperature exposure.
The intervention maintains stability during irradiation exposure.
The mechanical-performance improvement should hold under irradiation-exposed conditions.
Long-duration thermal stability of refractory high-entropy or refractory high-entropy-superalloy microstructures remains uncertain.
Long-duration irradiation stability of the proposed precipitate architecture remains uncertain.

contradictions.description: The stated performance baseline is a traditional single-principal-element alloy-design approach, whereas the experiment uses refractory high-entropy alloys without the precipitate sequence as its control. These are different comparisons, so the experiment does not directly test the stated baseline-relative prediction.
